Rule-Based Matching

Kenneth Benoit

2026-11-11

Source: vignettes/articles/matching.Rmd
matching.Rmd

Introduction

spacy_parse() returns what spaCy knows about each token: its lemma, its part of speech, its place in the dependency parse. Many questions about a text are about combinations of tokens: a passive verb, an adjective before a noun, a verb with its subject and object. spaCy answers these with rule-based matching, which finds the tokens that fit a pattern. spacyr has two functions for it:

  • spacy_extract_matches() finds sequences of adjacent tokens, using spaCy’s Matcher. It also matches phrases, and the values of a quanteda dictionary: if you have a list of phrases or a dictionary, go straight to Phrases and dictionaries.
  • spacy_extract_dependency_matches() finds tokens connected in the dependency parse, wherever they are in the sentence, using spaCy’s DependencyMatcher.

Both take patterns written as R lists, in the structure that spaCy documents in its guide to rule-based matching, and both return a data.frame. Neither changes the pipeline or the entities of a document: to turn matches into named entities, see the article on rule-based named entities.

library("spacyr")
spacy_initialize()
## successfully initialized (spaCy Version: 3.8.18, language model: en_core_web_sm)

Token patterns

A token pattern is a list with one element for each token, and each element is a named list of the attributes that the token must have. This pattern matches the two tokens “new” and “york”, in any case:

txt <- c(d1 = "New York is larger than York. I prefer new York.",
         d2 = "The New York Times is printed in New York.")
spacy_extract_matches(txt, list(NY = list(list(LOWER = "new"), list(LOWER = "york"))))
##   doc_id sentence_id token_id label     text start_id length
## 1     d1           1        1    NY New York        1      2
## 2     d1           2        3    NY new York       10      2
## 3     d2           1        2    NY New York        2      2
## 4     d2           1        8    NY New York        8      2

The name of the pattern, NY, is its label. For each match, the result has:

  • the document, and the sentence and token of the first token of the match, numbered as in spacy_parse();
  • the label and the matched text;
  • start_id, the position of the first token in the document, and length, the number of tokens.

Attributes can be any that spaCy sets on a token, including those that the language model assigns: LEMMA, POS and TAG for the part of speech, DEP for the dependency relation, and ENT_TYPE for the entity type. A token can also have an operator, OP, that says how often it may occur: "?" for optional, "+" for one or more, "*" for none or more. This pattern finds nouns with the adjectives before them:

ball <- "A big red shiny ball and a small blue box."
adj_noun <- list(ADJ_NOUN = list(list(POS = "ADJ", OP = "+"), list(POS = "NOUN")))
spacy_extract_matches(ball, adj_noun)
##   doc_id sentence_id token_id    label               text start_id length
## 1  text1           1        2 ADJ_NOUN big red shiny ball        2      4
## 2  text1           1        3 ADJ_NOUN     red shiny ball        3      3
## 3  text1           1        4 ADJ_NOUN         shiny ball        4      2
## 4  text1           1        8 ADJ_NOUN     small blue box        8      3
## 5  text1           1        9 ADJ_NOUN           blue box        9      2

Overlapping matches

That result has more rows than nouns, since spaCy returns every sequence that fits the pattern: “shiny ball” matches, and so do “red shiny ball” and “big red shiny ball”. This is the default, overlap = "all", so that nothing is left out unless you ask. With overlap = "longest", only the longest of the overlapping matches is kept, and with "first", the one that starts first:

spacy_extract_matches(ball, adj_noun, overlap = "longest")
##   doc_id sentence_id token_id    label               text start_id length
## 1  text1           1        2 ADJ_NOUN big red shiny ball        2      4
## 2  text1           1        8 ADJ_NOUN     small blue box        8      3

overlap applies to the matches of one label. Matches of different labels can still overlap.

Several patterns

A list can hold several patterns, each with its own label. A label can also have alternative patterns, given as a list of token patterns:

pats <- list(
  ADJ_NOUN = list(list(POS = "ADJ", OP = "+"), list(POS = "NOUN")),
  COLOUR = list(list(list(LOWER = "red")),
                list(list(LOWER = "blue")))
)
spacy_extract_matches(ball, pats, overlap = "longest")
##   doc_id sentence_id token_id    label               text start_id length
## 1  text1           1        2 ADJ_NOUN big red shiny ball        2      4
## 2  text1           1        3   COLOUR                red        3      1
## 3  text1           1        8 ADJ_NOUN     small blue box        8      3
## 4  text1           1        9   COLOUR               blue        9      1

The values that an attribute may take can be listed with IN, so the two colours could also be one pattern, list(list(LOWER = list(IN = c("red", "blue")))). Rows are in the order of the documents and, within a document, of the matches’ positions.

Example: passive verbs

Patterns can use the dependency relations that the parser assigns, which makes them a way to find grammatical constructions. The labels of these relations differ between language models, so the first step is to look at how the model in use parses an example. This is en_core_web_sm:

passive_txt <- c(p1 = "The book was written by Jane. Jane wrote the book.",
                 p2 = "Mistakes were made, and the report has not been finished.")
parsed <- spacy_parse(passive_txt, tag = TRUE, dependency = TRUE,
                      lemma = FALSE, entity = FALSE)
parsed[parsed$doc_id == "p1" & parsed$sentence_id == 1, ]
##   doc_id sentence_id token_id   token   pos tag head_token_id   dep_rel
## 1     p1           1        1     The   DET  DT             2       det
## 2     p1           1        2    book  NOUN  NN             4 nsubjpass
## 3     p1           1        3     was   AUX VBD             4   auxpass
## 4     p1           1        4 written  VERB VBN             4      ROOT
## 5     p1           1        5      by   ADP  IN             4     agent
## 6     p1           1        6    Jane PROPN NNP             5      pobj
## 7     p1           1        7       . PUNCT   .             4     punct

The English models label the auxiliary of a passive auxpass, and tag the past participle VBN. A pattern for a passive verb is then a passive auxiliary, any adverbs or negations in between, and a past participle:

passive <- list(
  PASSIVE = list(list(DEP = "auxpass"),
                 list(DEP = list(IN = c("advmod", "neg")), OP = "*"),
                 list(TAG = "VBN"))
)
spacy_extract_matches(passive_txt, passive)
##   doc_id sentence_id token_id   label          text start_id length
## 1     p1           1        3 PASSIVE   was written        3      2
## 2     p2           1        2 PASSIVE     were made        2      2
## 3     p2           1       10 PASSIVE been finished       10      2

It finds the three passives, and not “Jane wrote the book”. Because sentence_id and token_id are numbered as in spacy_parse(), matches can be joined to the parsed tokens on those two columns and doc_id:

matches <- spacy_extract_matches(passive_txt, passive)
joined <- merge(matches[, c("doc_id", "sentence_id", "token_id", "text")],
                parsed[, c("doc_id", "sentence_id", "token_id", "token", "dep_rel",
                           "head_token_id")])
joined[order(joined$doc_id, joined$sentence_id, joined$token_id), ]
##   doc_id sentence_id token_id          text token dep_rel head_token_id
## 1     p1           1        3   was written   was auxpass             4
## 3     p2           1        2     were made  were auxpass             3
## 2     p2           1       10 been finished  been auxpass            11

The position of a match is that of its first token, which here is the auxiliary, not the verb. The head_token_id of the auxiliary is the token_id of the verb it belongs to: token 4 of the first sentence of p1 is “written”.

The same columns count the sentences that have a passive in each document. p2 has two passive matches, but both are in its one sentence, so it counts once:

table(matches$doc_id)
## 
## p1 p2 
##  1  2
table(unique(matches[, c("doc_id", "sentence_id")])$doc_id)
## 
## p1 p2 
##  1  1

Phrases and dictionaries

Phrases are simpler to write than token patterns, and much faster to match when there are many of them. They are given as an as_entity_patterns() object, which records the label of each phrase and whether it matches exactly or in any case:

spacy_extract_matches(txt, as_entity_patterns(c(PLACE = "New York")))
##   doc_id sentence_id token_id label     text start_id length
## 1     d1           1        1 PLACE New York        1      2
## 2     d2           1        2 PLACE New York        2      2
## 3     d2           1        8 PLACE New York        8      2
spacy_extract_matches(txt, as_entity_patterns(c(PLACE = "New York"),
                                              case_insensitive = TRUE))
##   doc_id sentence_id token_id label     text start_id length
## 1     d1           1        1 PLACE New York        1      2
## 2     d1           2        3 PLACE new York       10      2
## 3     d2           1        2 PLACE New York        2      2
## 4     d2           1        8 PLACE New York        8      2

A quanteda dictionary can be given directly. Its top-level keys become the labels, so the values under nested keys take the label of the top-level key above them. Its values match in any case, with wildcards as in quanteda:

dict <- quanteda::dictionary(list(place = c("new york", "york"),
                                  size = c("larg*", "small*", "big*")))
spacy_extract_matches(txt, dict)
##    doc_id sentence_id token_id label     text start_id length
## 1      d1           1        1 place New York        1      2
## 2      d1           1        2 place     York        2      1
## 3      d1           1        4  size   larger        4      1
## 4      d1           1        6 place     York        6      1
## 5      d1           2        3 place new York       10      2
## 6      d1           2        4 place     York       11      1
## 7      d2           1        2 place New York        2      2
## 8      d2           1        3 place     York        3      1
## 9      d2           1        8 place New York        8      2
## 10     d2           1        9 place     York        9      1

Since “york” is itself a value, it also matches inside each “New York”. quanteda::tokens_lookup() counts such nested matches of a key once, and so does overlap = "longest" here; the default, overlap = "all", counts both. Choose one before comparing counts with quanteda’s:

table(spacy_extract_matches(txt, dict)$label)
## 
## place  size 
##     9     1
table(spacy_extract_matches(txt, dict, overlap = "longest")$label)
## 
## place  size 
##     5     1
quanteda::featfreq(quanteda::dfm(quanteda::tokens_lookup(quanteda::tokens(txt), dict)))
## place  size 
##     5     1

The counts can still differ for other texts, because the tokens are spaCy’s and not quanteda’s. What spacy_extract_matches() adds to a lookup is where each match is, in a form that joins to the output of spacy_parse(). A dictionary’s phrases and wildcard values can be combined with token patterns by converting it with as_entity_patterns() and joining the two with c().

Phrases are split into tokens by spaCy’s tokenizer, and match the same sequence of tokens in a text. spaCy sometimes splits a word differently in another case: it keeps "Inc." as one token, but splits "inc." into two. So a phrase written as "acme widgets, inc." does not match the text "Acme Widgets, Inc." even when it matches in any case, while the phrase "Acme Widgets, Inc." does:

inc <- "We wrote to Acme Widgets, Inc. yesterday."
nrow(spacy_extract_matches(inc, as_entity_patterns(c(ORG = "acme widgets, inc."),
                                                   case_insensitive = TRUE)))
## [1] 0
spacy_extract_matches(inc, as_entity_patterns(c(ORG = "Acme Widgets, Inc."),
                                              case_insensitive = TRUE))
##   doc_id sentence_id token_id label               text start_id length
## 1  text1           1        4   ORG Acme Widgets, Inc.        4      4

Dependency patterns

A token pattern finds tokens that are next to each other. The parts of a grammatical construction often are not: the subject of a passive verb can be many words before it. A dependency pattern describes tokens by their relations in the parse instead. It is a list of nodes, and each node is a named list with:

  • RIGHT_ID, a name for the node;
  • RIGHT_ATTRS, the attributes of the token, as in a token pattern;
  • for every node but the first, LEFT_ID, the name of an earlier node, and REL_OP, the relation between that node and this one. ">" means that this node is a direct dependent of the earlier one.

This pattern is a past participle, with a passive subject and a passive auxiliary as its dependents:

passive_dep <- list(
  list(RIGHT_ID = "verb", RIGHT_ATTRS = list(TAG = "VBN")),
  list(LEFT_ID = "verb", REL_OP = ">", RIGHT_ID = "subject",
       RIGHT_ATTRS = list(DEP = "nsubjpass")),
  list(LEFT_ID = "verb", REL_OP = ">", RIGHT_ID = "aux",
       RIGHT_ATTRS = list(DEP = "auxpass"))
)
m <- spacy_extract_dependency_matches(passive_txt, list(PASSIVE = passive_dep))
m
##   doc_id match_id   label    node sentence_id token_id start_id    token
## 1     p1        1 PASSIVE    verb           1        4        4  written
## 2     p1        1 PASSIVE subject           1        2        2     book
## 3     p1        1 PASSIVE     aux           1        3        3      was
## 4     p2        1 PASSIVE    verb           1        3        3     made
## 5     p2        1 PASSIVE subject           1        1        1 Mistakes
## 6     p2        1 PASSIVE     aux           1        2        2     were
## 7     p2        2 PASSIVE    verb           1       11       11 finished
## 8     p2        2 PASSIVE subject           1        7        7   report
## 9     p2        2 PASSIVE     aux           1       10       10     been

The result has one row for each node of the pattern in each match. node says which part of the pattern the token matched, and match_id numbers the matches within each document, so that doc_id and match_id together identify a match. Unlike the token pattern, this one also returns the subject of each passive, and finds the subject “report” although three words separate it from its verb.

To get one row for each match, with a column for each node, reshape the result:

wide <- reshape(m[, c("doc_id", "match_id", "node", "token")],
                idvar = c("doc_id", "match_id"), timevar = "node",
                direction = "wide")
names(wide) <- sub("^token\\.", "", names(wide))
wide
##   doc_id match_id     verb  subject  aux
## 1     p1        1  written     book  was
## 4     p2        1     made Mistakes were
## 7     p2        2 finished   report been

A pattern can follow the parse further. Adding the agent, “by” and its object, finds who did what to what, for the passives that say so:

agent <- c(passive_dep, list(
  list(LEFT_ID = "verb", REL_OP = ">", RIGHT_ID = "by",
       RIGHT_ATTRS = list(DEP = "agent")),
  list(LEFT_ID = "by", REL_OP = ">", RIGHT_ID = "agent",
       RIGHT_ATTRS = list(DEP = "pobj"))
))
m <- spacy_extract_dependency_matches(passive_txt, list(PASSIVE_AGENT = agent))
m[m$node %in% c("subject", "verb", "agent"), c("doc_id", "node", "token")]
##   doc_id    node   token
## 1     p1    verb written
## 2     p1 subject    book
## 5     p1   agent    Jane

Each label has one dependency pattern, so alternatives, such as passives with and without an agent, get labels of their own. The other relations that REL_OP can take, such as ">>" for a dependent at any depth and "." for the next token, are listed in spaCy’s documentation.

What to keep in mind

Labels belong to the model. The tags and dependency labels above are those of spaCy’s English models. Other languages’ models use other labels, and some do not mark the passive at all. Look at the output of spacy_parse(x, tag = TRUE, dependency = TRUE) for the model you use before writing a pattern.

A match is only as good as the parse. The model tags and parses by prediction, and makes mistakes. It also makes choices that a pattern has to follow. Here the second verb of a coordination, “edited”, is attached to the first as conj and has no subject or auxiliary of its own, so neither passive pattern above finds it:

coord <- "The book was written and edited by Jane."
spacy_extract_matches(coord, passive)
##   doc_id sentence_id token_id   label        text start_id length
## 1  text1           1        3 PASSIVE was written        3      2
spacy_extract_dependency_matches(coord, list(PASSIVE = passive_dep))[, c("node", "token")]
##      node   token
## 1    verb written
## 2 subject    book
## 3     aux     was

A further pattern, for a participle coordinated with a passive verb, finds it:

conj <- list(
  list(RIGHT_ID = "first", RIGHT_ATTRS = list(TAG = "VBN")),
  list(LEFT_ID = "first", REL_OP = ">", RIGHT_ID = "aux",
       RIGHT_ATTRS = list(DEP = "auxpass")),
  list(LEFT_ID = "first", REL_OP = ">", RIGHT_ID = "verb",
       RIGHT_ATTRS = list(TAG = "VBN", DEP = "conj"))
)
spacy_extract_dependency_matches(coord, list(PASSIVE_CONJ = conj))[, c("node", "token")]
##    node   token
## 1 first written
## 2   aux     was
## 3  verb  edited

Testing patterns on examples of the constructions you want, and of those you do not, is the way to find such cases.

The pipeline has to set what a pattern asks for. A pattern on DEP needs the parser, and a dependency pattern needs a dependency parse; both give an error without one. A pattern on ENT_TYPE gives a warning when no component sets entities, as after spacy_initialize(entity = FALSE), since it would match nothing.

Speed

Matching adds little to the time that spaCy takes to parse the texts. On a test with 5,000 sentences, a dictionary of 10,000 phrases and several hundred wildcard values took no longer than a single token pattern. Token patterns are slower in large numbers, since spaCy checks each one against the text: give phrases as phrases, not as token patterns, when there are thousands of them.

Patterns that do not use entities are faster after spacy_initialize(entity = FALSE), which leaves out the named entity recognizer. spacy_initialize() does nothing while spaCy is running, as it has been since the start of this article, so call spacy_finalize() first:

spacy_finalize()
spacy_initialize(entity = FALSE)
## successfully initialized (spaCy Version: 3.8.18, language model: en_core_web_sm)
spacy_extract_matches(passive_txt, passive)
##   doc_id sentence_id token_id   label          text start_id length
## 1     p1           1        3 PASSIVE   was written        3      2
## 2     p2           1        2 PASSIVE     were made        2      2
## 3     p2           1       10 PASSIVE been finished       10      2
spacy_finalize()

See the article on improving performance for more on this, and for n_process and batch_size, which both functions also take.
